extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exercises for improvisers and teachers on creating emotional change, using gibberish/physical offers, status exchanges, and provocations to generate dramatic and comic scenes. Includes specific games (gibberish switch, four-line gibberish, paperflicking) and coaching notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fight the instinct to look sane / display large emotional changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisers should resist the social habit of 'looking sane' and instead make large, fluctuating emotional choices onstage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We teach children to look sane; improvisers must fight this instinct. Encourage big, rapid emotional changes (as adults do only when drunk). If you realize you’ve lost your job or been humiliated, reach for new, raw emotion rather than a funny line. Coaches should encourage sustaining the emotion and praise students who do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify and sustain big emotional responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Big emotional reactions must be justified by the scene and sustained long enough to drive the scene forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try playing someone drunk to practice emotional fluidity. Make offers that will elicit big emotions in others. If partners don't respond, be emotional about their lack of response. Heap detailed praise when improvisers manage to sustain strong emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Somebody must be changed (story requires change)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene 'won't seem like a story unless somebody is changed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change can be sudden or gradual; dramatic effect often comes from playing all your aces at once. Use status transfers or emotional reversals so the audience perceives risk and vulnerability. Teach change as a primary objective of storytelling in improv.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status Exchange / dramatic status change as a technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberately change characters' status (e.g., senior interviewer losing all status at once) to create striking, story-driving moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: instruct an interviewer to put their head in their hands and start crying—lose all status at once—so the candidate must get an answer explaining why, referencing earlier material. Once mastered, use pair-work and locations (hospital, church) so students invent characters and see the technique's power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gibberish must sound like speech and imply mutual understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: When speaking gibberish, it should sound like real speech (varied sounds, not repetitive) and actors must behave as if they understand each other perfectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid weak-tea, consonant-free utterances; use accents and varied phonetics. Demonstrate and practice en masse so anxious students can rehearse out of the spotlight. Encourage experimentation with different 'accents'—whatever works for the player.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enthusiasm and playfulness are key for gibberish
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers should present gibberish exercises with cheerful enthusiasm to lower anxiety and promote playful risk-taking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce the game energetically and demonstrate. Let everyone practice together and pick someone who looks like they’re having fun to perform a toast or joke. Optionally label the game 'advanced' to excuse struggle, but enthusiasm generally works better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure: short four-line gibberish scenes for practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a structured four-line (two lines each) gibberish exercise in lines to let many players try brief scenes and encourage variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form two lines of players; front pair step up and perform a four-line gibberish scene, then return to the back. Encourage different accents and experimentation. After a dozen or so, pause to compare which interactions worked and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key rule: have a reaction to your partner’s lines
rubrics_metrics.description: The crucial mechanism in gibberish (and many scenes) is reacting to what your partner 'said' rather than trying to define what they said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do exercises where one line is neutral and the partner chooses an arbitrary reaction; the first player then reacts to that. If neither character is affected, 'nothing has happened' and there is no story. Teach players to make choices that affect them and to use partner reactions as the source of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use English/gibberish 'switch' to change state and physicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Switching between English and gibberish mid-scene changes volume, physicality, emotional commitment and can unstick habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run scenes speaking English, then yell 'Switch!' to change to gibberish and back repeatedly, shortening intervals to blur modes. Observe that gibberish makes players louder, more physical and committed; English lets you define relationships and specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not translate gibberish (avoid Foreign Film Dub pitfalls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translating gibberish destroys the game's risk and the illusion of communication; the translator often becomes the focus and kills spontaneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign Film Dub requires gibberish actors to pause and wait for a translator, which prevents instant reactions and creates confusion. Translators feel pressured to be clever and may block physical offers. Avoid having gibberish translated; if you want the benefits of both modes, switch between them instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mime props can establish place but may destroy the illusion of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Using mime props can clarify location/situation but can prevent the audience from believing two people are speaking a common (made-up) language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mime props are useful to set place, but Spolin's approach emphasizes action over translation. Use mime thoughtfully; recognize it may break the illusion of 'language' if you pantomime everything.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeating the other person’s words is a useful trick but not essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Echoing a partner can help create the illusion of communication in gibberish scenes but should be one tool among many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out repetition as a counter to slack gibberish with few consonants. Give partners opportunities to pick out and repeat 'words' where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: In gibberish, infer meaning from partner’s reaction rather than striving for literal sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the words are unintelligible, actors should look to their partner’s tone and physical reaction to deduce what was 'said' and respond accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the partner looks shocked, you probably insulted them; if they hug you, you probably told them they're pregnant. This creates a sweep of story even with obscure detail—use partner cues as meaning-makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use English to define relationships and specifics—don’t repeat obvious offers
rubrics_metrics.description: When returning to English, use the opportunity to define relationships or advance story details, rather than restating what was already clear in gibberish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in gibberish someone spills coffee, don't switch to English and say 'You just spilled your coffee.' Instead, use English to add new stakes or demands (e.g., 'There is just one way you can make this up to me...'). English segments should define rather than duplicate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gibberish scenes need both sensitivity and boldness; persist with training
rubrics_metrics.description: Playing an entire scene in gibberish is challenging; groups need perseverance to develop sensitivity to offers and boldness to commit to emotional change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect initial struggle; keep practicing. Successful groups gain exquisite sensitivity to partners' offers and willingness to stride boldly into new directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gibberish as a litmus test for a game’s worth
rubrics_metrics.description: If a game is worth playing in gibberish, it is probably worth playing in English; if it fails in gibberish, it likely won’t work in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the gibberish version to evaluate what a game emphasizes (e.g., Word-At-A-Time gibberish emphasizes physicality and commitment). The gibberish variant often illuminates what the English version should emphasize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperflicking / provocation: raise stakes and ensure the target is affected
rubrics_metrics.description: When introducing a private provocation (e.g., interviewer secretly tearing CV and flicking pieces) the dramatic point is to make the candidate suffer—so the candidate must be affected for the scene to work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the instruction to the provoker in private. Make sure the scene establishes platform (job, qualifications) and that the candidate has reason to want the job (desperation raises stakes). If the candidate refuses to be affected, the scene flatlines. Re-run with coaching to encourage being affected; once the candidate reacts, the scene leaps into life and forces the provoker to mentally edit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep private instructions subtle—don’t over-direct players out of inventing environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit stage directions like 'Tear up the CV' can discourage the instructed player from adding environmental detail; private quirks should provoke without replacing creative input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When giving private instructions, avoid removing the player's need to contribute to environment or character. Over-prescriptive directions can flatten improvisational contribution elsewhere (analogy: smoothing a sheet creates wrinkles elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish platform and stakes before introducing complications
rubrics_metrics.description: Before adding quirks or provocations, ensure the basic platform (what the job is, candidate qualifications) and stakes are clear so the audience and players understand what’s to lose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up the interview context and the candidate’s need for the job; otherwise the provocation has less dramatic weight and the audience won’t appreciate the risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using humor to belittle strong emotions; treat strong emotion seriously
rubrics_metrics.description: Making jokes about strong emotions often belittles them, reassures the joke-maker, and produces poor drama and weak comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sensitive coach will encourage improvisers to treat situations seriously and praise them when they sustain authentic emotion. Joke-making can be a coping mechanism that prevents powerful, truthful performance.
